Q055-IgA-nephropathy.stem:
A 12-year-old boy presents to the General Practice clinic with his parent after noticing dark-coloured urine for two days. He has had a sore throat and runny nose for the past four days. He has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. His immunisations are up to date.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 85/min, blood pressure 118/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. His throat is erythematous with enlarged tonsils. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 1+ protein.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Q055-IgA-nephropathy.rationale:
This patient presents with the classic features of IgA nephropathy: macroscopic haematuria occurring simultaneously with an upper respiratory tract infection (synpharyngitic haematuria). IgA nephropathy is the most common form of glomerulonephritis worldwide and typically presents in children and young adults.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can present similarly but typically occurs 1-2 weeks after a streptococcal infection (post-infectious), not during the infection. It also usually presents with more systemic features including hypertension and oedema.

Thin basement membrane disease can cause persistent microscopic haematuria but rarely causes episodes of macroscopic haematuria. It is an inherited condition that usually presents in childhood with isolated microscopic haematuria.

Alport syndrome is an inherited condition that causes progressive kidney disease with haematuria, but it typically presents with persistent microscopic haematuria and associated features such as hearing loss and eye abnormalities.

Acute interstitial nephritis typically presents with acute kidney injury, often in association with medication use (particularly antibiotics or NSAIDs). While it can cause haematuria, the timing with upper respiratory tract infection is more suggestive of IgA nephropathy.

The definitive diagnosis of IgA nephropathy requires a kidney biopsy showing mesangial IgA deposits. However, in a patient with typical presentation and mild disease (normal blood pressure, minimal proteinuria), observation with regular monitoring may be appropriate initially.

IgA nephropathy commonly presents with macroscopic haematuria coinciding with upper respiratory tract infections (synpharyngitic haematuria).
The presence of proteinuria and hypertension in IgA nephropathy indicates more severe disease.
Renal biopsy showing mesangial IgA deposits is required for definitive diagnosis of IgA nephropathy.
Q055-IgA-nephropathy.learning:
IgA nephropathy commonly presents with macroscopic haematuria coinciding with upper respiratory tract infections (synpharyngitic haematuria).
The presence of proteinuria and hypertension in IgA nephropathy indicates more severe disease.
Renal biopsy showing mesangial IgA deposits is required for definitive diagnosis of IgA nephropathy.

Q058-IgA-nephropathy.stem:
A 35-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a one-day history of darkening of his urine. He had an upper respiratory tract infection five days ago for which he did not take any medication and is currently recovering. He has a history of recently-diagnosed Type 2 diabetes mellitus which is diet-controlled. He takes no regular medications. On physical examination, all vital signs are within normal limits and no skin rash is detected.

His urine test results are shown:

Protein = +1

Glucose = Negative

Ketones = Negative

Leucocyte esterase = Negative

Nitrites = Negative

Crystals = None

RBC = 50/HPF

White blood cells = 7/HPF

Casts = RBC casts present

Serum complement levels are normal.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Q058-IgA-nephropathy.rationale:
This patient with dark urine five days after an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) and signs of nephritic syndrome (eg, mild proteinuria, haematuria) are consistent with the diagnosis of IgA nephropathy (IgAN). IgAN presents with recurrent episodes of gross or microscopic haematuria typically within days after a URTI.

Another common differential that is associated with glomerulonephritis after a URTI is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). However, patients usually present with PSGN two to three weeks after an URTI. In addition, PSGN is more common in children, whereas IgAN is more common in adults aged 20-30 years. C3 is usually reduced in PSGN and typically normal in IgAN.

Acute interstitial nephritis is an acute inflammation of renal interstitium and tubules after exposure to certain medications (eg, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, penicillins, sulphonamides). Patients can also have a fever, joint pains, skin rash, and eosinophilia.

Diabetic nephropathy typically affects patients with a long-standing history of diabetes (and/or poorly controlled diabetes) and commonly presents with proteinuria, but not haematuria as in this patient, making this option less likely.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis typically presents with a nephrotic syndrome picture, not haematuria seen in this patient.

Haematuria and recent respiratory infection should always raise the possibility of an IgA nephropathy.
Q058-IgA-nephropathy.learning: Haematuria and recent respiratory infection should always raise the possibility of an IgA nephropathy.

Q137-IgA-nephropathy.stem:
A 26-year-old man presents to the General Practice clinic with a two-day history of dark red urine. He has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. He reports three similar episodes over the past two years, with the most recent occurring six months ago and resolving spontaneously. He has had coryzal symptoms including sore throat and non-productive cough for three days.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 90/min, blood pressure 160/105 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. Urinalysis reveals blood 3+ and protein 1+.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Q137-IgA-nephropathy.rationale:
This patient presents with the classic features of IgA nephropathy, which is the most common form of glomerulonephritis worldwide. The key diagnostic features are recurrent episodes of visible haematuria that typically occur during or immediately following an upper respiratory tract infection, often called synpharyngitic haematuria. The patient's age, gender, and pattern of presentation are highly characteristic.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura is also mediated by IgA but typically presents with additional features including palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain. The absence of these extra-renal manifestations makes this diagnosis less likely.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically occurs 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal infection, not during the acute infection. It is more common in children and usually presents as a single episode rather than recurrent episodes.

Goodpasture syndrome is characterised by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies and typically presents with concurrent pulmonary haemorrhage (manifesting as haemoptysis) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The absence of pulmonary symptoms and the recurrent nature of symptoms make this diagnosis unlikely.

Alport syndrome is an inherited condition affecting type IV collagen. While it can cause haematuria, it typically presents in childhood and is associated with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities. The late onset and absence of these associated features make this diagnosis unlikely.

IgA nephropathy classically presents with episodes of visible haematuria during or immediately after upper respiratory tract infections.
Recurrent episodes of visible haematuria with concurrent infections suggest IgA nephropathy rather than other forms of glomerulonephritis.
Hypertension is a common finding in IgA nephropathy and may indicate chronic kidney damage.
Q137-IgA-nephropathy.learning:
IgA nephropathy classically presents with episodes of visible haematuria during or immediately after upper respiratory tract infections.
Recurrent episodes of visible haematuria with concurrent infections suggest IgA nephropathy rather than other forms of glomerulonephritis.

Q032-Anti-streptolysin-O-titre.stem:
A nine-year-old Aboriginal boy presents to the General Practice clinic with a three-day history of puffy eyes and face, particularly noticeable in the mornings. His mother reports that his urine appears dark. Two weeks ago, he had a sore throat that resolved without treatment. He has no significant medical history and does not take any regular medications. His immunisations are up to date.

On examination, he appears mildly unwell with periorbital and facial oedema. His pulse rate is 90/min, blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.0°C. There is mild pitting oedema of the ankles. Throat examination reveals no erythema or exudate. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein, and specific gravity 1.025.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
Q032-Anti-streptolysin-O-titre.rationale:
This patient presents with the classic triad of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN): oedema, hypertension, and haematuria. The timing of symptoms approximately two weeks after a sore throat is consistent with APSGN following streptococcal pharyngitis. APSGN is an immune complex-mediated disease that occurs following infection with nephritogenic strains of Group A Streptococcus.

Anti-streptolysin O titre is the most appropriate next investigation as it provides evidence of recent streptococcal infection. ASO titres begin to rise approximately one week after streptococcal infection and peak at 3-5 weeks. A positive ASO titre in the context of this clinical presentation would strongly support the diagnosis of APSGN. Anti-DNase B is another serological marker that can be used, particularly in cases following skin infections.

Renal biopsy is the gold standard for definitive histological diagnosis of APSGN but is invasive and not indicated as the initial investigation in a straightforward presentation. It is reserved for atypical cases, those with a prolonged or deteriorating course, or when the diagnosis remains uncertain after non-invasive workup.

Renal ultrasound is not typically necessary for the initial diagnosis of APSGN. While it may show enlarged, echogenic kidneys, these findings are non-specific and would not confirm the diagnosis. Renal ultrasound would be more appropriate if there were concerns about other causes of acute kidney injury or if the clinical course was atypical.

Throat swab culture is unlikely to be positive at this stage, as the streptococcal pharyngitis typically precedes APSGN by 1-2 weeks. By the time nephritis develops, the throat infection has often resolved, as appears to be the case in this patient.

24-hour urine protein collection would provide quantification of proteinuria but is not necessary for the initial diagnosis of APSGN. The urinalysis already demonstrates proteinuria, and while nephrotic-range proteinuria can occur in APSGN, establishing the link to streptococcal infection is more diagnostically valuable at this stage.

Management of APSGN typically involves supportive care, including salt and fluid restriction if oedema is present, and antihypertensive therapy if blood pressure remains elevated. Antibiotics are recommended to eradicate any remaining streptococcal infection, even if cultures are negative. Most children with APSGN have an excellent prognosis with complete recovery, although a small percentage may develop chronic kidney disease.

Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically presents with oedema, hypertension, and haematuria approximately 1-4 weeks after streptococcal infection.
Urinalysis showing haematuria, proteinuria, and red cell casts is characteristic of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Elevated anti-streptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titres confirm recent streptococcal infection in suspected acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Q070-Antistreptolysin-O-titre.stem:
A seven-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a one-week history of facial puffiness and dark-coloured urine. He has no significant medical history and does not take any regular medications. His parents report that he had a sore throat about three weeks ago, which resolved without treatment.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 90/min, blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. There is periorbital oedema and mild pitting oedema of the lower limbs. Urinalysis reveals haematuria and proteinuria. Blood tests show elevated serum creatinine of 120 μmol/L (45-90) and urea of 10 mmol/L (2.5-6.5).

Which one of the following is the next best investigation to assist with diagnosis?
Q070-Antistreptolysin-O-titre.rationale:
The clinical presentation in this case is highly suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The patient has a history of a recent sore throat, followed by the classic triad of oedema, hypertension, and abnormal urinalysis (haematuria and proteinuria) about three weeks later. These features, along with the elevated creatinine and urea, strongly support this diagnosis.

The antistreptolysin O titre (ASOT) is the next best investigation to assist with confirming the diagnosis. ASOT is used to detect recent streptococcal infections, which are the most common cause of post-infectious glomerulonephritis in children. ASOT levels typically rise 1-2 weeks after the initial infection and remain elevated for several months, making it an ideal test in this scenario where the throat infection occurred three weeks prior.

Serum complement levels, particularly C3, are often low in acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. However, while supportive of the diagnosis, they are not specific for confirming a recent streptococcal infection. C3 levels typically normalise within 6-8 weeks.

A renal biopsy is an invasive procedure and is not routinely required to diagnose post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis when the clinical presentation is typical, as in this case. It may be considered in atypical presentations or when the diagnosis is uncertain.

A urine culture would not be helpful in confirming a recent streptococcal throat infection. It is more relevant for diagnosing urinary tract infections, which is not the likely diagnosis given the clinical picture.

A throat swab for streptococcal antigen is unlikely to be positive at this stage, as the throat infection occurred three weeks ago. Streptococcal antigens are typically only detectable during the acute phase of the infection or shortly thereafter.

In summary, while all these investigations may have a role in the workup of glomerulonephritis, the ASOT is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in this clinical scenario.

Antistreptolysin O titre (ASOT) is used to confirm a recent streptococcal infection in the context of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically presents 1-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection with oedema, hypertension, and abnormal urinalysis.
Q070-Antistreptolysin-O-titre.learning:
Antistreptolysin O titre (ASOT) is used to confirm a recent streptococcal infection in the context of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Q020-Proteinase-3-anti-neutrophil-cytopl.stem:
A 56-year-old woman is referred to the hospital nephrology service for investigation of proteinuria and microscopic haematuria. She has developed progressive renal impairment over the past two months, with a current estimated glomerular filtration rate of 25 mL/min/1.73m2 (>90). She reports recurrent sinusitis over the past year and gradual onset of hearing loss. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications.

On examination, her pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C. She has a saddle nose deformity. A renal biopsy has been arranged.

Which one of the following laboratory tests is most likely to be positive?
Q020-Proteinase-3-anti-neutrophil-cytopl.rationale:
This patient presents with features highly suggestive of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), a type of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis. The combination of renal involvement (proteinuria, haematuria, rapidly progressive renal impairment), upper respiratory tract manifestations (saddle nose deformity, recurrent sinusitis), and sensorineural hearing loss constitutes the classic presentation. The classic triad of GPA includes upper respiratory tract disease, lung involvement, and glomerulonephritis. Early recognition and treatment with immunosuppression is crucial to prevent irreversible organ damage.

Proteinase 3 anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (PR3-ANCA) is the most likely positive test, as it is present in approximately 70-90% of patients with active, generalised GPA. The presence of upper respiratory tract involvement, particularly saddle nose deformity from nasal cartilage destruction, is highly characteristic of GPA and strongly favours PR3-ANCA positivity over other serological markers.

Myeloperoxidase anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (MPO-ANCA) are more commonly associated with microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. While MPO-ANCA can occasionally be positive in GPA, the prominent upper respiratory tract involvement in this patient makes PR3-ANCA far more likely.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are associated with anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, which typically presents with pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. This condition does not cause upper respiratory tract destruction, sinusitis, or hearing loss, making it inconsistent with this clinical picture.

Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. While lupus nephritis can cause proteinuria and haematuria, the upper respiratory tract involvement with saddle nose deformity would be atypical, and other features such as malar rash, arthralgia, and serositis would typically be expected.

Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies are specific for primary membranous nephropathy, which presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria. This condition would not account for the systemic manifestations seen in this patient, particularly the upper respiratory tract disease.

The following table summarises the key serological associations and distinguishing features of these conditions:

Antibody	Associated condition	Key distinguishing features
PR3-ANCA	Granulomatosis with polyangiitis	Upper airway destruction, sinusitis, lung nodules/cavities, glomerulonephritis
MPO-ANCA	Microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis	Glomerulonephritis, pulmonary capillaritis; lacks upper airway granulomatous disease
Anti-glomerular basement membrane	Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease	Pulmonary haemorrhage, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; no upper airway disease
Anti-double stranded DNA	Systemic lupus erythematosus	Malar rash, arthralgia, serositis, cytopaenias, nephritis
Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor	Primary membranous nephropathy	Nephrotic syndrome without systemic vasculitic features
PR3-ANCA is strongly associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, particularly in patients with upper respiratory tract involvement such as saddle nose deformity and sinusitis.
The classic triad of granulomatosis with polyangiitis includes upper respiratory tract disease, lung involvement, and glomerulonephritis.
Q020-Proteinase-3-anti-neutrophil-cytopl.learning:
PR3-ANCA is strongly associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, particularly in patients with upper respiratory tract involvement such as saddle nose deformity and sinusitis.
