Q121-Anti-glomerular-basement-membrane-a.stem:
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a seven-day history of coughing up approximately one teaspoon of blood daily. He also reports fatigue, decreased urine output, and tea-coloured urine over the past three days. He has no significant medical history and does not take any regular medications. He is a current smoker with an eight pack-year history. He recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection two weeks ago.

On examination, he appears unwell. His pulse rate is 96/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral fine crackles in the lower zones. There is mild bilateral pedal oedema.

Investigations reveal a haemoglobin of 98 g/L (130–175), white cell count 9.2 × 109/L (4.0–11.0), platelet count 260 × 109/L (150–400), urea 18.4 mmol/L (3.0–9.5), serum creatinine 480 µmol/L (60–110), and estimated glomerular filtration rate 12 mL/min/1.73m2 (>90). A chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein, and red blood cell casts.

Which one of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
Q121-Anti-glomerular-basement-membrane-a.rationale:
This patient presents with a classic pulmonary-renal syndrome characterised by haemoptysis, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (rising creatinine, haematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell casts), and diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates on chest X-ray. The combination of pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis in a young man who smokes strongly suggests glomerular basement membrane disease (previously known as Goodpasture syndrome). Smoking is a well-recognised risk factor for pulmonary involvement in this condition, as it increases alveolar capillary permeability. The rapid decline in renal function with an active urinary sediment containing red blood cell casts indicates severe glomerular injury.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are the confirmatory test for glomerular basement membrane disease. These autoantibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the basement membranes of the glomeruli and pulmonary alveoli, leading to rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. The clinical picture of concurrent pulmonary and renal involvement in a young smoker with red blood cell casts is highly characteristic of this condition.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are used to diagnose small-vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis, which can also present with a pulmonary-renal syndrome. However, the rapid onset of severe renal failure with concurrent pulmonary haemorrhage in a young smoker without other systemic features such as sinusitis, skin vasculitis, or neuropathy makes glomerular basement membrane disease more likely.

Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies are associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus and stiff-person syndrome. They are not relevant to a pulmonary-renal presentation.

Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are typically found in autoimmune hepatitis and are not associated with pulmonary or renal disease of this nature.

Anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibodies are associated with mixed connective tissue disease, which may involve multiple organ systems but does not typically present with this acute combination of alveolar haemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Glomerular basement membrane disease presents with a pulmonary-renal syndrome of haemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, confirmed by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.
Red blood cell casts on urinalysis indicate glomerular injury and help distinguish glomerulonephritis from other causes of haematuria.
Q121-Anti-glomerular-basement-membrane-a.learning:
Glomerular basement membrane disease presents with a pulmonary-renal syndrome of haemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, confirmed by anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.
Red blood cell casts on urinalysis indicate glomerular injury and help distinguish glomerulonephritis from other causes of haematuria.

Q113-Renal-biopsy.stem:
A 60-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a three-day history of coughing up small quantities of fresh blood. He has also experienced pleuritic chest pain and increasing breathlessness. He feels generally unwell and feverish. He has no significant medical history and does not take any regular medications.

On examination, he appears unwell. His pulse rate is 90/min, blood pressure 124/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% on room air, and temperature 37.8°C. There is reduced air entry bilaterally with dull percussion notes at both lung bases.

Investigations reveal:

Haemoglobin 120 g/L (115-155)
Platelets 200 × 109/L (150-450)
White cell count 10.0 × 109/L (4.0-10.0)
Creatinine 150 μmol/L (60-110)
Sodium 135 mmol/L (137-145)
Potassium 4.5 mmol/L (3.5-4.9)

Urinalysis shows blood ++, no protein, no leucocytes, no nitrates. Red cell casts are present on urinary sediment.

Which one of the following is the most definitive diagnostic test?
Q113-Renal-biopsy.rationale:
The clinical picture - together with the laboratory results - show evidence of a pulmonary and renal problem, both suggesting anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease; also known as Goodpasture syndrome.

Anti-GBM disease is a rare small vessel vasculitis that affects the capillary beds of the kidneys and lungs. It is an autoimmune condition that is caused by development of autoantibodies against autoantigen expressed in the basement membranes of these organs although the full pathogenesis is not fully understood. Most patients develop widespread glomerular crescent formation, presenting with features of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and about 40%–60% will have concurrent alveolar haemorrhage. Red cell casts are highly abnormal and point towards glomerular bleeding.

The other possible unifying diagnoses for his haemoptysis and glomerulonephritis (often termed 'pulmonary-renal syndrome') are vasculitis due to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lupus, and microscopic polyangiitis; all of which could potentially be diagnosed with the renal biopsy.

Renal biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test for anti-GBM disease. It allows direct visualization of glomerular damage and, most importantly, immunofluorescence studies can demonstrate the linear deposition of IgG antibodies along the glomerular basement membrane, which is pathognomonic for the condition. Renal biopsy can also help diagnose other causes of pulmonary-renal syndrome such as ANCA-associated vasculitis or lupus nephritis.

ANCA levels would be helpful in diagnosing ANCA-associated vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener's granulomatosis) or microscopic polyangiitis, which can also present with pulmonary-renal syndrome. However, anti-GBM disease can sometimes exist in the absence of circulating antibodies, and approximately 30% of patients with anti-GBM disease are also ANCA positive, making this test less definitive than renal biopsy.

Chest X-ray may show bilateral alveolar infiltrates in pulmonary haemorrhage but is non-specific and cannot differentiate between the various causes of pulmonary-renal syndrome. It may be useful as an initial investigation but is not definitive.

CT Pulmonary Angiogram would be useful to exclude pulmonary embolism, which can present with pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis. However, it would not explain the urinary findings and would not be diagnostic for anti-GBM disease or other vasculitides.

Pleural tap would not be diagnostic in this case as the primary pathology is alveolar haemorrhage rather than pleural effusion. Even if pleural fluid were present, analysis would not provide a definitive diagnosis for the underlying condition.

Anti-GBM disease is a rare autoimmune condition where antibodies target antigens in the basement membranes of the lungs and kidneys. It typically presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage. Early diagnosis and treatment with plasma exchange, corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide are crucial to prevent irreversible kidney damage and life-threatening pulmonary haemorrhage.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) presents with pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.
Red cell casts in urine are highly suggestive of glomerular bleeding.
Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence is the definitive diagnostic test for anti-GBM disease.
Q113-Renal-biopsy.learning:
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) presents with pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.
Red cell casts in urine are highly suggestive of glomerular bleeding.
Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence is the definitive diagnostic test for anti-GBM disease.

Q010-ANCA-associated-vasculitis.stem:
A 55-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a two-week history of fatigue, joint pain, and frothy urine. She has noticed her ankles are swollen and her urine appears dark. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications.

On examination, she appears unwell. Her pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 165/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, and temperature 37.8°C. She has bilateral pitting ankle oedema. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein.

Blood tests reveal:

Creatinine 250 µmol/L (45-90)
Urea 15.0 mmol/L (2.5-7.0)
Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155)

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Q010-ANCA-associated-vasculitis.rationale:
This patient presents with features of nephritic syndrome (haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and reduced renal function) along with systemic symptoms including fatigue, joint pain, and fever. The acute presentation with multi-system involvement strongly suggests a vasculitic process.

ANCA-associated vasculitis typically presents with constitutional symptoms (fatigue, fever, weight loss), musculoskeletal involvement (arthralgia, myalgia), and renal involvement (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). The combination of active urinary sediment, reduced renal function, and systemic symptoms makes this the most likely diagnosis.

Amyloidosis typically presents with nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) rather than nephritic syndrome. While it can affect multiple organs, it usually has a more indolent course and rarely presents with active inflammation or joint pain.

Thin basement membrane disease is typically benign, presenting with isolated microscopic haematuria. It does not cause systemic symptoms or significant proteinuria. It rarely causes reduced renal function.

Membranous nephropathy characteristically presents with nephrotic syndrome. While it can have an associated systemic disease, it typically does not present with significant haematuria or systemic inflammation.

Minimal change disease presents with pure nephrotic syndrome, typically without haematuria or reduced renal function. It is more common in children and young adults, and rarely associated with systemic symptoms.

Nephritic syndrome is characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and renal impairment.
Q010-ANCA-associated-vasculitis.learning: Nephritic syndrome is characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and renal impairment.

Q049-Renal-biopsy.stem:
A 29-year-old woman presents for her routine follow-up. She had complains of joint pain and swelling for which she is under treatment. Her medical history includes systemic lupus erythematosus. On examination her blood pressure is 142/98 mmHg, pulse 86/min and temperature 37.1oC. She has a rash on her cheeks and there is diffuse tenderness and swelling of her finger joints.

Routine investigation shows a white cell count of 8.6 x 10*9/L (4 - 11) with a lymphocyte count of 0.9 x 10*9/L ,1.0 - 3.5). Routine urinalysis shows proteinuria, microscopic haematuria, red blood cells and red blood cell casts.

Which one of the following investigations will be most appropriate in assisting in diagnosis and management?
Q049-Renal-biopsy.rationale:
The above given urinalysis in a patient with SLE are suggestive of lupus nephritis, a common complication of SLE. Lupus nephritis is an inflammation of the kidneys, a type of glomerulonephritis caused by systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disease. Renal biopsy is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis and grading of lupus nephritis. It helps to determine the extent and severity of kidney damage as well as assists in treatment decisions, such as the use of immunosuppressive therapy.

Ultrasound KUB may help detect abnormalities in the urinary tract, such as hydronephrosis, kidney stones, cysts etc. but it has no specific role in lupus nephritis.

Renal function tests are a series of blood tests that assess the function of the kidneys, including tests for creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). While it can help to assess the severity of kidney damage and monitor the progression of kidney disease, it is not specific for lupus nephritis. In this case, a renal biopsy would be a more definitive test to confirm the diagnosis of lupus nephritis and guide treatment decisions.

Intravenous pyelogram is an imaging test that involves injecting a contrast dye into the veins and taking X-rays to visualise the urinary tract. While it can help to detect structural abnormalities in the kidneys and urinary tract, such as obstruction or tumours, it also has no significant role in lupus nephritis.

24-hour urine protein is a test that quantifies the amount of protein excreted in the urine over a 24-hour period. It helps in assessing the severity of proteinuria and monitor the progression of nephrotic and nephritic syndrome but not of lupus nephritis while the biopsy helps in grading and planning treatment.

Renal biopsy is the gold standard investigation for lupus nephritis.
Q049-Renal-biopsy.learning: Renal biopsy is the gold standard investigation for lupus nephritis.

Q080-Dapagliflozin.stem:
A 28-year-old Aboriginal female is admitted to hospital with a two-month history of joint pain and fatigue. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, her pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. She has oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia and synovitis in the small joints in both hands. Investigations reveal multiple abnormalities including positive antinuclear antibodies with a titre of 1:640 and sub-nephrotic range proteinuria. Following confirmation of the diagnosis on renal biopsy, she receives intravenous methylprednisolone followed by a high-dose oral prednisolone tail, hydroxychloroquine, and mycophenolate sodium.

Which of the following medications is LEAST appropriate to be initially commenced alongside steroids?
Q080-Dapagliflozin.rationale:
This patient presents with features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) including oral ulcers, alopecia, arthritis, and lupus nephritis confirmed on biopsy. She is being treated with high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppression, which necessitates several preventive medications.

Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor used for various indications including diabetes management and reduction of proteinuria in various forms of kidney disease. Whilst close monitoring of BSLs (especially in the afternoon) is vital in patients commenced on high-dose steroids, immediately commencing an agent such as an SGLT2 inhibitor is inappropriate given the potential for risks without definitive confirmation of persistent hyperglycaemia. Such risks of SGLT2 inhibitors include urinary tract infections, which may be particularly harmful in an already immunosuppressed patient. Of course, if monitoring of BSLs revealed steroid-induced hyperglycaemia, an agent such as intermediate-acting insulin may be appropriate in the first instance, in consultation with an endocrinologist.

Esomeprazole is appropriate as prophylaxis against steroid-induced reflux and gastric ulceration, which is a significant risk with high-dose corticosteroids. Proton pump inhibitors are recommended for all patients receiving high-dose steroids.

Colecalciferol (vitamin D) and calcium carbonate are essential for minimising the risk of steroid-induced osteoporosis. All patients on long-term corticosteroids should receive calcium and vitamin D supplementation unless contraindicated.

Trimethoprim / Sulfamethoxazole is appropriate as prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, a severe opportunistic infection in immunosuppressed patients. This is particularly important given the combination of high-dose steroids and mycophenolate.

The management of lupus nephritis requires careful attention to preventing complications of both the disease and its treatment. While immunosuppression is necessary to control disease activity, preventive measures against infection, osteoporosis, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease are equally important aspects of care.

With regards to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population, there exists an increased incidence of SLE compared to non-Indigenous people. There also exists an increased rate of lupus nephritis as a manifestation of SLE, as well as increased rates of progression to end-stage kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with lupus nephritis.

While immunosuppression is necessary to control disease activity in lupus nephritis, preventive measures against infection, osteoporosis, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease are equally important aspects of care
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.
Q080-Dapagliflozin.learning:
While immunosuppression is necessary to control disease activity in lupus nephritis, preventive measures against infection, osteoporosis, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease are equally important aspects of care
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.

Q117-Optical-coherence-tomography.stem:
A 28-year-old Aboriginal female is admitted to hospital with a two-month history of joint pain and fatigue. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, her pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. She has oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia and synovitis in the small joints in both hands. Investigations reveal multiple abnormalities including positive antinuclear antibodies with a titre of 1:640 and sub-nephrotic range proteinuria. Following confirmation of the diagnosis on renal biopsy, she receives intravenous methylprednisolone followed by a high-dose oral prednisolone tail, hydroxychloroquine, and mycophenolate sodium.

Which one of the following monitoring investigations is most important whilst this patient is taking hydroxychloroquine?
Q117-Optical-coherence-tomography.rationale:
This patient has been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with lupus nephritis as a manifestation on renal biopsy, and appropriately commenced on hydroxychloroquine as part of their management regimen. Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial medication commonly used in SLE that can cause irreversible retinal toxicity, making regular ophthalmological screening essential.

Optical coherence tomography is currently considered the most sensitive test for early detection of hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy. It can detect subtle changes in the retinal layers before clinical symptoms develop. Guidelines recommend baseline screening within the first year of treatment and then annual screening after five years of use, or sooner in high-risk patients.

Full blood examination monitoring is important for patients on immunosuppressive medications like mycophenolate, but it is not the most critical test for hydroxychloroquine specifically. While hydroxychloroquine can rarely cause blood dyscrasias, this is not its main toxicity concern.

Thyroid function tests are not routinely required for hydroxychloroquine monitoring. Transthoracic echocardiogram is important in SLE patients to monitor for complications like pericarditis or valve disease, but it is not specifically required for hydroxychloroquine monitoring. Liver function tests are routinely monitored in patients on multiple medications, particularly with mycophenolate, but hepatotoxicity is not a major concern with hydroxychloroquine.

Regarding hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy, early detection through regular screening is crucial as retinal damage can progress even after cessation of the medication.

With regards to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population, there exists an increased incidence of SLE compared to non-Indigenous people. There also exists an increased rate of lupus nephritis as a manifestation of SLE, as well as increased rates of progression to end-stage kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with lupus nephritis.

Hydroxychloroquine requires regular ophthalmological screening due to risk of retinopathy.
Optical coherence tomography is the most sensitive test for early detection of hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy.
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.
Q117-Optical-coherence-tomography.learning:
Hydroxychloroquine requires regular ophthalmological screening due to risk of retinopathy.
Optical coherence tomography is the most sensitive test for early detection of hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy.
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.

Q132-Renal-doppler-ultrasound.stem:
A 28-year-old Aboriginal female is admitted to hospital with a two-month history of joint pain and fatigue. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, her pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.2°C. She has oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia and synovitis in the small joints in both hands. Investigations reveal multiple abnormalities including positive antinuclear antibodies with a titre of 1:640 and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

Which one of the following would be LEAST helpful in identifying renal involvement in this condition?
Q132-Renal-doppler-ultrasound.rationale:
This patient presents with features suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), including oral ulcers, non-scarring alopecia, synovitis, positive ANA, and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Lupus nephritis is a common and serious manifestation of SLE that requires early identification and management.

Renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing and classifying lupus nephritis. It provides crucial information about the histological subtype of lupus nephritis and severity of kidney involvement, which guides treatment decisions and prognosis.

24-hour urine collection and urine albumin-creatinine ratio are both valid methods for quantifying proteinuria, which is a key marker (and the most common abnormality) seen in lupus nephritis. Whilst 24-hour urine collection provides a more accurate quantification of proteinuria, the collection process is not always practical, hence a spot urine albumin-creatinine ratio can provide a quick and reasonable accurate measure of proteinuria.

Urine microscopy is essential as it can reveal active urinary sediment, including dysmorphic red blood cells, which is an indicator of active lupus nephritis.

Renal doppler ultrasound is the least helpful investigation for identifying lupus nephritis. While it may show kidney size and exclude obstruction, it does not provide specific information about lupus nephritis activity or classification. Changes in renal blood flow are neither sensitive nor specific for lupus nephritis.

When screening for lupus nephritis, it is important to assess for renal impairment (serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate), proteinuria (either by spot ratio test or 24hour urine collection) and microscopic haematuria (urine microscopy). If clinical suspicion is combined with any of the above abnormalities, strong consideration should be given to renal biopsy.

With regards to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population, there exists an increased incidence of SLE compared to non-Indigenous people. There also exists an increased rate of lupus nephritis as a manifestation of SLE, as well as increased rates of progression to end-stage kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with lupus nephritis.

When screening for lupus nephritis, it is important to assess for renal impairment, proteinuria and microscopic haematuria.
If clinical suspicion is combined with any of the above abnormalities, strong consideration should be given to renal biopsy.
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.
Q132-Renal-doppler-ultrasound.learning:
When screening for lupus nephritis, it is important to assess for renal impairment, proteinuria and microscopic haematuria.
If clinical suspicion is combined with any of the above abnormalities, strong consideration should be given to renal biopsy.
There are higher rates of SLE and lupus nephritis in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population.

Q141-Lupus-anticoagulant.stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the nephrology clinic for routine follow-up of her lupus nephritis. She was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) five years ago and developed lupus nephritis two years ago. Her regular medications include hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisolone. She has no new symptoms and feels well.

On examination, she appears well. Her pulse rate is 72/min, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. There are no significant findings on physical examination.

Which one of the following laboratory tests is LEAST useful for monitoring lupus nephritis activity?
Q141-Lupus-anticoagulant.rationale:
In monitoring lupus nephritis activity, several laboratory tests are used in combination with clinical assessment to track disease progression and response to therapy.

Lupus anticoagulant is an antiphospholipid antibody that, while associated with SLE, does NOT correlate with kidney inflammation or damage in lupus nephritis. Its presence or absence provides no useful information about nephritis activity, making it the least useful test for monitoring.

Proteinuria is one of the most sensitive markers for monitoring lupus nephritis activity. Quantitative measures such as urine protein-to-creatinine ratio directly reflect glomerular injury and respond quickly to changes in disease activity.

Complement C3 level is a valuable serological marker that typically decreases during active disease due to consumption in immune complex formation. Low complement levels often correlate with active lupus nephritis and tend to normalize with successful treatment.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, while non-specific, provides useful information about overall inflammatory activity in SLE. When interpreted alongside other markers, it contributes to the assessment of disease activity.

Serum creatinine is important for monitoring kidney function in lupus nephritis, though changes may lag behind other markers. Significant elevations often indicate more severe or chronic kidney damage.

Other useful monitoring tests include anti-dsDNA antibodies, which often correlate with disease activity. The most effective monitoring strategy combines clinical assessment with both urinary markers (especially proteinuria) and serological markers (complement levels and anti-dsDNA antibodies).

Lupus anticoagulant testing is not useful for monitoring lupus nephritis activity as it does not correlate with kidney inflammation.
Proteinuria and complement levels are the most sensitive markers for monitoring lupus nephritis activity.
A comprehensive monitoring approach should include clinical assessment, urinary markers, and serological markers.
Q141-Lupus-anticoagulant.learning:
Lupus anticoagulant testing is not useful for monitoring lupus nephritis activity as it does not correlate with kidney inflammation.
Proteinuria and complement levels are the most sensitive markers for monitoring lupus nephritis activity.
A comprehensive monitoring approach should include clinical assessment, urinary markers, and serological markers.

Q013-Hepatitis-C.stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to the General Practice clinic with one month of ankle swelling. He has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, his pulse rate is 78/min, blood pressure 165/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. He has bilateral pitting ankle oedema. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable.

Investigations reveal:

Serum creatinine: 120 µmol/L (60-110)
Albumin: 28 g/L (35-50)
Urinary protein/creatinine ratio: 280 mg/mmol (<30)
Dysmorphic red cells seen on urine microscopy

A renal biopsy shows membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with subendothelial and mesangial immune deposits.

Which one of the following liver conditions is most commonly associated with this renal diagnosis?
Q013-Hepatitis-C.rationale:
This patient presents with proteinuria, microscopic haematuria, hypertension and mild renal impairment, and has been found to have membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) on renal biopsy. MPGN can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to various conditions, with chronic infections being a major cause.

Hepatitis C infection is the most common cause of secondary MPGN in adults. The association is thought to be due to the deposition of circulating immune complexes containing hepatitis C antigens.

Primary biliary cholangitis can be associated with various forms of glomerulonephritis, but MPGN is not typically associated with this condition. The most common renal manifestation of PBC is tubulointerstitial nephritis.

Alcohol-related liver disease is not typically associated with MPGN. While it can cause various renal complications, these are usually related to cirrhosis and portal hypertension rather than immune complex deposition.

Hepatitis B infection can cause various forms of glomerulonephritis, but membranous nephropathy is more commonly associated with hepatitis B than MPGN.

Autoimmune hepatitis can be associated with various forms of glomerulonephritis, but MPGN is not a typical manifestation. IgA nephropathy is more commonly seen in autoimmune hepatitis.

The diagnosis of MPGN should prompt investigation for underlying causes, particularly hepatitis C. Other conditions associated with MPGN include chronic bacterial infections (such as endocarditis), autoimmune diseases (such as systemic lupus erythematosus), and monoclonal gammopathies.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is commonly associated with chronic hepatitis C infection.
Q013-Hepatitis-C.learning: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is commonly associated with chronic hepatitis C infection.

Q014-Normal-glomeruli.stem:
A 7-year-old boy presents to his General Practice clinic with his parents with progressive swelling of his face for two days. He experienced an upper respiratory tract infection seven days ago. His past medical history is otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, his vitals are within the normal range. On examination, there is mild oedema detected in the lower extremities. The examination of other systems is normal. Investigations show a normal complete blood count, renal function tests and liver function tests. Urine examination shows proteinuria and oval fatty bodies are seen on microscopy. A 24-hour urine collection test gives the value of protein to be 3.7 g/day. Ultrasound of the abdomen is unremarkable. A kidney biopsy is ordered.

Which one of the following histological findings is most likely to be seen in this patient on light microscopy?

options.text: Apple green birefringence under polarized light
Crescents of fibrin and monocytes in glomeruli

Q014-Normal-glomeruli.rationale:
This patient with oedema, proteinuria >3.5 g per day, and fatty casts is suffering from nephrotic syndrome. Minimal change disease (MCD) is a type of nephrotic syndrome that is more common in children aged <10 years and is often idiopathic. A few cases may present following an infection (as seen in this patient), immunisation, or any other immune stimulus.

MCD is postulated to result from cytokine-mediated injury to the foot processes of podocytes. This disrupts the negative charge of the glomerular basement membrane, allowing albumin to leak into the renal tubules and be excreted in the urine. Decreased albumin levels lead to decreased oncotic pressure in vessels, resulting in oedema.

Since this disease is mainly due to disruption of the charge barrier, urinalysis shows only proteinuria. Haematuria is not seen in a nephrotic syndrome. Fatty casts/oval fat bodies may also be seen on microscopy. Light microscopy of the histologic sample obtained from a kidney biopsy may reveal normal glomeruli. Immunofluorescence studies are unremarkable, while electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.

Amyloid deposition in the mesangium shows apple-green birefringence when the histologic sample is stained with Congo red and viewed under polarised light. Systemic amyloidosis results in this disease. This patient has no history or signs or symptoms of diseases resulting in amyloidosis (e.g., multiple myeloma, IBD, etc).

Glomeruli containing crescents consisting of fibrin, monocytes, macrophages, and other plasma proteins are seen in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). However, it is a nephritic syndrome and is associated with rapidly deteriorating renal function.

Eosinophilic nodular glomerulosclerosis (i.e. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) is a feature of diabetic nephropathy. This patient's young age, with no history or signs or symptoms of diabetes, makes this diagnosis highly unlikely.

Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis also develops after group A streptococcal infection (e.g., pharyngitis, impetigo) and is characterised by hypercellularity and glomerular enlargement. However, it is a nephritic syndrome and is characterised by hypertension, haematuria, and RBC casts in urine.

Minimal change disease (MCD) is a type of nephrotic syndrome that is more common in children aged <10 years and is often idiopathic.
Q014-Normal-glomeruli.learning: Minimal change disease (MCD) is a type of nephrotic syndrome that is more common in children aged <10 years and is often idiopathic.

Q027-Minimal-change-disease.stem:
A 20-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a two-week history of progressive swelling around his eyes and legs. He reports decreased urine output and frothy urine. He has no significant medical history and does not take any regular medications. His immunisations are up to date.

On examination, he appears unwell. His pulse rate is 100/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. There is periorbital and pedal oedema. Abdominal examination reveals mild ascites.

Investigations reveal:

Urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood
Serum albumin: 18 g/L (35–50)
Serum creatinine: 40 µmol/L (60–110)
Total cholesterol: 7.2 mmol/L (<5.5)

A renal biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows no significant glomerular abnormality. Electron microscopy reveals diffuse podocyte foot process effacement. Immunofluorescence is negative.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Q027-Minimal-change-disease.rationale:
This patient presents with the classic features of nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria (4+ on urinalysis), hypoalbuminaemia (18 g/L), hyperlipidaemia (total cholesterol 7.2 mmol/L), and generalised oedema including periorbital and pedal oedema with ascites. The renal biopsy findings are critical in distinguishing between the causes of nephrotic syndrome. In this case, the combination of normal light microscopy, diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, and negative immunofluorescence is pathognomonic for minimal change disease.

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and remains a significant cause in young adults. It characteristically shows no glomerular abnormality on light microscopy, with the only finding being diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Immunofluorescence is typically negative, with no immunoglobulin or complement deposition. The preserved renal function (serum creatinine 40 µmol/L), absence of haematuria, and the patient's age are all consistent with this diagnosis. Minimal change disease typically responds well to corticosteroid therapy.

Membranous nephropathy is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in older adults. It is characterised by thickening of the glomerular basement membrane on light microscopy and subepithelial immune complex deposits on electron microscopy, with granular IgG and C3 staining on immunofluorescence. These features are absent in this case.

IgA nephropathy typically presents as a nephritic syndrome with haematuria, often following an upper respiratory tract infection. Renal biopsy would show mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence and mesangial proliferation on light microscopy. The absence of haematuria and negative immunofluorescence make this diagnosis unlikely.

IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that can cause renal involvement with IgA deposition in the glomerular mesangium, similar to IgA nephropathy. It typically presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain in addition to renal manifestations, and would show mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence. None of these features are present in this case.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis can present similarly to minimal change disease with nephrotic syndrome and foot process effacement on electron microscopy. However, it is distinguished by the presence of focal and segmental areas of sclerosis on light microscopy, which are not seen in this case. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is also more likely to be associated with haematuria, hypertension, and impaired renal function.

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and young adults, characterised by foot process effacement on electron microscopy with normal light microscopy findings.
The classic presentation of nephrotic syndrome includes heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, and oedema.
Q027-Minimal-change-disease.learning:
Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and young adults, characterised by foot process effacement on electron microscopy with normal light microscopy findings.
The classic presentation of nephrotic syndrome includes heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, and oedema.

Q037-Focal-segmental-glomerulosclerosis.stem:
A 35-year-old man presents with a two-month history of headache, facial swelling, and ankle swelling. On further questioning, he has noticed frothy, but normal coloured, urine. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 10 years ago, for which he takes metformin. He ceased intravenous drug use six months ago.

On examination, his blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 99% on room air. There is bilateral pitting oedema of his ankles. Chest examination reveals clear breath sounds bilaterally with no signs of respiratory distress. The abdominal examination indicates a soft, non-tender abdomen without hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.

A urine dipstick demonstrates 3+ proteinuria and his blood tests show an albumin level of 22g/L (32-45g/L). A renal biopsy is performed which shows:

light microscopy: segmental obliteration of the glomerular tuft

electron microscopy: effacement of foot processes

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: light microscopy: segmental obliteration of the glomerular tuft
electron microscopy: effacement of foot processes

Q037-Focal-segmental-glomerulosclerosis.rationale:
Based on the provided clinical presentation and results of his investigations, the correct diagnosis is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). The characteristic features such as intravenous drug use history, peripheral oedema, frothy urine, pitting oedema, hypertension, proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, with the specific renal pathology observed on electron microscopy (foot process effacement and segmental obliteration of the glomerular tuft) are consistent with FSGS.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is characterised by localised scarring in glomeruli and commonly associated with nephrotic syndrome and hypertension. It can affect individuals of various ages, including adults. In the context of the provided case, the gradual onset of symptoms, electron microscopy findings of foot process effacement, and segmental obliteration align well with FSGS, making this the likely diagnosis.

Intravenous (IV) drug use is linked to FSGS due to the direct nephrotoxic effects of substances injected, such as heroin. The injected substances may induce immune complex formation, depositing in the glomeruli and causing inflammation. Additionally, renal ischaemia resulting from IV drug use contributes to glomerular injury and scarring. FSGS is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome, characterised by proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia, with specific histological changes like foot process effacement observed on electron microscopy.

Minimal change disease (MCD) is a primary glomerular disorder typically observed in children, with its hallmark manifestation being generalised oedema, proteinuria, and hypoalbuminaemia. This condition often has an abrupt onset and is marked by the absence of significant changes in renal histology visible under light microscopy. Unlike the presented case, MCD rarely involves hypertension and is more commonly diagnosed in paediatric populations.

Membranous nephropathy involves immune complex deposition in the glomerular basement membrane, typically presenting with nephrotic syndrome. However, hypertension and foot process effacement, as seen in the electron microscopy findings of the patient, are not typical features of this condition. Membranous nephropathy is more commonly diagnosed in adults.

Typically, diabetic nephropathy develops over an extended period in individuals with longstanding diabetes, with microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome. . Renal biopsies in diabetic nephropathy typically reveal diffuse glomerulosclerosis under light microscopy, with thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and expansion of the mesangium. On electron microscopy, characteristic findings include the presence of nodular glomerulosclerosis, thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, and mesangial expansion.

IgA nephropathy, characterised by the deposition of IgA immune complexes in the glomerular mesangium, is considered less likely in this case due to the absence of haematuria. Typically, IgA nephropathy presents with recurrent episodes of gross or microscopic haematuria. However, in this case, there is no mention of any signs of haematuria. Moreover, the renal biopsy findings in the case reveal segmental obliteration of the glomerular tuft and foot process effacement, which are not typical features associated with IgA nephropathy, known for mesangial proliferation. The absence of key diagnostic features makes IgA nephropathy a less probable explanation for the patient's condition. In IgA nephropathy, light microscopy often shows mesangial proliferation and the presence of IgA deposits, while electron microscopy reveals mesangial immune complex deposits.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) typically presents with nephrotic syndrome (oedema, nephrotic range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia).
Q037-Focal-segmental-glomerulosclerosis.learning: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) typically presents with nephrotic syndrome (oedema, nephrotic range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia).

Q038-Venous-thromboembolism.stem:
A 64-year-old man from South Africa is referred to the nephrologist with symptoms of persistent leg swelling and frothy urine. The patient has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity and sickle cell disease. On examination his blood pressure is 141/95 mmHg, pulse 82/min and temperature 37.0oC. Urinalysis shows +++ for proteins without haematuria. Urinary PCR is 800mg/mmol (60-300). Blood glucose and haemoglobin are at normal levels; blood work analysis shows the following abnormalities:

Urea: 14mmol/L (2.5–7.8)

Creatinine: 145μmol/L (59–104)

eGFR: 63 (>90)

Albumin: 12g/L (35–50)

Additional testing shows the presence of anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies and kidney biopsy is shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane with IgG and C3 deposits in a spike and dome appearance.

If left untreated, which one of the following complications is this patient most at risk of?
Q038-Venous-thromboembolism.rationale:
Based on the findings of the patient's urinalysis, this patient is showing signs of massive proteinuria (above 3.5g/day), without haematuria. Therefore, this patient has a nephrotic syndrome. This patient has membranous nephropathy. Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome which predominantly affects older males of Caucasian descent; elevated blood pressure is a risk factor for this condition. The condition is generally classified as either primary or secondary. Secondary causes of membranous nephropathy include infections such as syphilis, malignancy, usage of specific medications such as penicillin and NSAIDS. Primary membranous nephropathy is caused by the presence of anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies, which is present in this patient. A kidney biopsy with "a spike and dome appearance," with the presence of a thickened glomerular basement membrane, IgG and deposits of C3 is confirmatory for this condition. Patients with this condition can present with chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidaemia, hyper-coagulability, and signs of AKI, such as low GFR, high creatinine, and low albumin. Treatment for this condition includes the usage of ACEi/ARBs, prednisolone, and cyclophosphamide; monoclonal antibodies may be used in refractory cases.

Of all the listed potential complications, this patient is most at risk of venous thromboembolism, as membranous nephropathy places patients in a hypercoaguable state. If left unaddressed for a long period of time, this can start as a deep vein thrombosis and eventually progress to a pulmonary embolism. Notably, deep vein thrombosis has been shown to occur more commonly in patients with membranous nephropathy compared to other nephrotic conditions. Other major complications of membranous nephropathy are hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and end-stage renal failure.

Recurrent infections may occur in membranous nephropathy - however, this tends to be due to the usage of immunotherapy/cyclophosphamide to treat the membranous nephropathy, as opposed to the condition itself. Recurrent infections may also occur in minimal change disease due to loss of IgG, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Similarly, thrombotic microangiopathy may also occur in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; this is a thrombosis that may occur in the capillaries and/or arterioles as a result of endothelial injury. Bladder cancer is not likely to occur due to membranous nephropathy, but instead may occur due to the usage of cyclophosphamide. Hypertensive encephalopathy is a hypertensive emergency that also occurs alongside a changed mental status, and is likely to be a consequence of a nephritic syndrome as opposed to a nephrotic syndrome.

Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome characterised by massive proteinuria, hyperlipidaemia, hyper-coagulability, and signs of AKI.
If left unaddressed, membranous nephropathy can lead to end-stage renal failure, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and hyperlipidaemia
Cyclophosphamide is a treatment for membranous nephropathy, but has potential side-effects such as recurrent infections and bladder cancer.
Q038-Venous-thromboembolism.learning:
Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome characterised by massive proteinuria, hyperlipidaemia, hyper-coagulability, and signs of AKI.
If left unaddressed, membranous nephropathy can lead to end-stage renal failure, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and hyperlipidaemia
Cyclophosphamide is a treatment for membranous nephropathy, but has potential side-effects such as recurrent infections and bladder cancer.

Q088-Subepithelial-immune-complex-deposi.stem:
A 45-year-old man presents to the General Practice clinic with a two-month history of leg swelling, facial swelling, and frothy urine. He also reports increased fatigue. He has no shortness of breath, nausea, or vomiting. He has a medical history of chronic hepatitis B and hypertension. His regular medications are tenofovir and ramipril.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 80/min, blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 37.0°C. There is bilateral periorbital oedema and bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, with markedly oedematous feet and ankles. There is no ascites and his chest is clear. Heart sounds are dual with no murmurs.

Investigations reveal:

Urine dipstick: protein 4+, blood negative
Serum albumin: 18 g/L (35-50)
Serum creatinine: 95 µmol/L (60-110)
Total cholesterol: 9.2 mmol/L (<5.5)

A renal biopsy is performed.

Which one of the following is the most likely finding on electron microscopy of the kidney biopsy?

options.text: Diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane

Q088-Subepithelial-immune-complex-deposi.rationale:
This patient presents with nephrotic syndrome, characterised by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and peripheral oedema. In the context of chronic hepatitis B infection, the most likely underlying glomerular disease is membranous nephropathy. Hepatitis B is one of the most well-recognised secondary causes of membranous nephropathy, in which hepatitis B antigens form immune complexes that deposit along the glomerular basement membrane. Treatment of the underlying hepatitis B with tenofovir is essential, and ramipril (an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) helps to reduce proteinuria.

Subepithelial immune complex deposits on the glomerular basement membrane are the hallmark finding of membranous nephropathy on electron microscopy. These deposits form between the podocyte foot processes and the outer surface of the glomerular basement membrane, leading to basement membrane thickening and disruption of the filtration barrier. This is the most likely diagnosis given the nephrotic syndrome presentation and the association with hepatitis B.

Mesangial immune complex deposits are the characteristic finding of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, which is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. However, it typically presents with haematuria (often macroscopic haematuria following an upper respiratory tract infection) rather than isolated heavy proteinuria and full nephrotic syndrome. The absence of blood on urine dipstick makes this diagnosis less likely.

Diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane is seen in thin basement membrane nephropathy, a benign condition that typically presents with persistent microscopic haematuria and minimal proteinuria. It does not cause nephrotic syndrome and is not associated with hepatitis B.

Subendothelial immune complex deposits are characteristic of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (type I) and certain classes of lupus nephritis. While hepatitis B can occasionally be associated with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy is the far more common association. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis more often presents with a nephritic picture including haematuria and low complement levels.

Intramembranous electron-dense deposits are the defining feature of dense deposit disease (previously known as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type II). This is a rare condition that typically presents in childhood or early adulthood and is associated with complement pathway dysregulation rather than hepatitis B infection.

Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults with chronic hepatitis B and is characterised by subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy.
Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and oedema.
Q088-Subepithelial-immune-complex-deposi.learning:
Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults with chronic hepatitis B and is characterised by subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy.
Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and oedema.

Q097-Phospholipase-A2-receptor-PLA2R-ant.stem:
A 55-year-old woman presents to the General Practice clinic with a three-week history of progressive bilateral leg swelling. She has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, she appears well. Her pulse rate is 78/min, blood pressure 158/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. There is pitting oedema to both knees.

Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Investigations reveal serum albumin 28 g/L (35-50), total cholesterol 7.2 mmol/L (2.0-5.0), and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 560 mg/mmol (<15). The patient undergoes a renal biopsy, where light microscopy demonstrates a thickened basement membrane, and there is diffuse granular glomerular basement membrane staining on immunofluorescence.

Which one of the following investigations is most useful in differentiating between the primary and secondary cause of this disease?
Q097-Phospholipase-A2-receptor-PLA2R-ant.rationale:
Please note that this question is beyond the expected level of a graduating medical student, however contains very useful learning content so has been kept in the question back.

This patient presents with clinical features of nephrotic syndrome (oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and proteinuria) and has biopsy findings consistent with membranous nephropathy. The key question is how to differentiate between primary (idiopathic) and secondary membranous nephropathy.

Phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibody testing is the most useful investigation for this purpose. PLA2R antibodies are highly specific (>95%) for primary membranous nephropathy and are present in about 70-80% of patients with this condition. The presence of these antibodies strongly suggests primary membranous nephropathy, while their absence points towards a secondary cause.

Complement C3 and C4 levels are not specific for membranous nephropathy. While they may be low in some secondary causes (e.g., lupus nephritis), they are not helpful in differentiating primary and secondary causes as definitively as PLA2R testing.

Urine albumin-creatinine ratio is a measure of albuminuria (similar to urine protein-creatinine ratio but only for albumin), which would be expected to be elevated given the high UPCR. Whilst this test is useful for quantifying proteinuria, it does not help differentiate between primary and secondary causes of membranous nephropathy.

Beta-2 glycoprotein antibody is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome. It is not helpful in differentiating primary and secondary causes of membranous nephropathy.

Urine microscopy for cast analysis can provide information about kidney damage but doesn't specifically differentiate between primary and secondary membranous nephropathy.

PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy.
Nephrotic syndrome is a common presentation of membranous nephropathy.
Q097-Phospholipase-A2-receptor-PLA2R-ant.learning:
PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy.
Nephrotic syndrome is a common presentation of membranous nephropathy.

Q064-Amyloid-light-chain-nephropathy.stem:
A 68-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS) now presents with sudden onset, bilateral swelling of his legs. In addition, he also noticed bruising around his eyes and an inability to raise his hands over his head. His medical history is significant for obesity for which he manages through lifestyle modifications.

On examination he has prominent, rounded protrusions over the anterior aspect of his deltoid muscles. His tongue also appears large. He has bilateral pitting oedema to the level of his knee. His blood pressure is 137/74 mmHg, pulse 84/min temperature 37.3C, respiratory rate 14/min and SpO2 98% on room air.

A dipstick urinalysis returned +++ proteinuria. A 24-hour urine protein is returned as 5.2g/24 hours. Serum HbA1c is returned as 4.5% and albumin is 24g/L (normal: 32-45 g/L).

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for his renal impairment?
Q064-Amyloid-light-chain-nephropathy.rationale:
The triad of macroglossia, shoulder pad sign and raccoon eye, in combination with the presence of nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5g/24 hours and background of plasma cell dyscrasia, should raise suspicion for light chain amyloidosis (AL). AL is a systemic disease that causes amyloid light chain protein deposition within different organs, including the kidney and heart.

Minimal change disease is another cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is less likely to be the patient's diagnosis given his significant history and symptoms.

Diabetic nephropathy can also cause nephrotic syndrome, but is only seen in patients with progressive diabetes. His serum HbA1c is 4.5%, which indicates good glycaemic control over the past 3 months. He was not diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a systemic ANCA positive vasculitis that predominately affects the respiratory tract and kidneys. It usually does not manifest with nephrotic syndrome on first appearance; rather patients would have microscopic haematuria and a gradual decline in renal function.

IgA nephropathy rarely causes nephrotic syndrome. Rather, it usually presents with microscopic or macroscopic haematuria a few days after a non-specific upper respiratory tract infection.

In patients presenting with nephrotic syndrome on a background of plasma cell dyscrasia, amyloidosis should be suspected
Q064-Amyloid-light-chain-nephropathy.learning: In patients presenting with nephrotic syndrome on a background of plasma cell dyscrasia, amyloidosis should be suspected

Q073-Prednisolone.stem:
A six-year-old boy presents to his General Practice clinic with his mother with a two-month history of generalised swelling, particularly around his ankles. His mother has also noticed frothy urine and that he has gained about 4 kg in weight. He has no significant medical history and is up to date with immunisations.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 88/min, blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 13/min, and temperature 38.6°C. There is mild bilateral pitting oedema on his lower extremities and some periorbital oedema. His chest is clear with no added sounds. A 24-hour urine protein measurement shows 4 g of protein.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
Q073-Prednisolone.rationale:
The patient has presented with signs and symptoms of nephrotic syndrome, which is confirmed by the presence of 4 g protein in a 24-hour urine sample. In children, nephrotic-range proteinuria is defined as protein excretion greater than 40 mg/m2/hour (or greater than 1 g/m2/day), whilst normal protein excretion is less than 4 mg/m2/hour (or less than 100 mg/m2/day). Prednisolone, a corticosteroid, is the first-line treatment option for patients with nephrotic syndrome. The exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, but it is believed that corticosteroids regulate nuclear gene expression via the cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor, activating genes for anti-inflammatory cytokines and suppressing genes for pro-inflammatory cytokines. For this reason, the Royal Children's Hospital (RCH) guidelines identify corticosteroids as the treatment for disease management.

The presence of fever (38.6°C) in this child with nephrotic syndrome is concerning, as it may indicate an underlying infection. Children with nephrotic syndrome are at increased risk of infections due to urinary losses of immunoglobulins and the immunosuppressive effects of corticosteroid treatment. Therefore, while initiating prednisolone therapy, it is crucial to promptly evaluate and treat any potential infection.

Furosemide, a diuretic, can help in removing oedematous fluid, especially when it is causing symptoms. However, it does not resolve the underlying pathology and is not used as a first-line treatment option for nephrotic syndrome. In cases of severe or symptomatic oedema, furosemide might be considered as an initial treatment, but that is not the case here. For this patient, RCH guidelines recommend a strict fluid balance, sodium and fluid restriction, and intermittent concentrated albumin infusions to manage oedema; IV furosemide may be used in conjunction with albumin but should be used cautiously as it may precipitate intravascular volume depletion, acute kidney injury and increase risk of thrombosis.

Rituximab, an anti-B cell antibody, can be used for the treatment of steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome. However, it is not a first-line drug, and a trial of steroids should be given initially.

Cyclosporin, a calcineurin inhibitor, is used in patients with steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome. In cases of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, calcineurin inhibitors are the first-line choice, and other agents are employed if there is no response.

Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, is used in patients with secondary nephrotic syndrome, such as that secondary to diabetic nephropathy. By reducing proteinuria, these drugs lead to reduced intraglomerular pressure, causing a reduction in systemic blood pressure.

Corticosteroids are the first-line treatment option for nephrotic syndrome.
Fever in a child with nephrotic syndrome may indicate an underlying infection, which requires prompt evaluation and treatment.

Corticosteroids are the first-line treatment option for nephrotic syndrome.
Fever in a child with nephrotic syndrome may indicate an underlying infection, which requires prompt evaluation and treatment.

Q077-Oral-prednisolone.stem:
A seven-year-old boy presents to the General Practice clinic with a three-week history of puffy eyes and swollen legs. He has no significant medical history and takes no regular medications. His immunisations are up to date.

On examination, he appears well. His pulse rate is 85/min, blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. He has periorbital and peripheral oedema. His urine dipstick shows 3+ protein.

Blood tests reveal:

Albumin 28 g/L (35-50)
Creatinine 45 µmol/L (20-60)
Cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L (2.8-4.8)

A renal biopsy confirms focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
Q077-Oral-prednisolone.rationale:
This child presents with nephrotic syndrome, characterised by oedema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and hypercholesterolaemia. The renal biopsy confirms focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), which accounts for approximately 10-20% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in children.

Oral prednisolone is the first-line treatment for FSGS in children. The typical regimen involves daily prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) for 4-8 weeks, followed by alternate-day therapy if there is a response. Response to steroids is the most important prognostic factor in childhood FSGS.

Cyclosporine is typically reserved as second-line therapy for steroid-resistant cases. While effective, it requires careful monitoring of drug levels and renal function, and has significant side effects including nephrotoxicity and hypertension.

Cyclophosphamide may be considered in steroid-resistant cases, but its use is limited by significant side effects including bone marrow suppression and increased risk of infections. It is not appropriate as first-line therapy.

Mycophenolate mofetil is sometimes used as a steroid-sparing agent in children who have responded to initial steroid therapy but become steroid-dependent. It would not be appropriate as initial therapy.

Rituximab is generally reserved for cases that have failed multiple other therapies. Its role in primary FSGS is still being evaluated, and it would not be appropriate as first-line treatment.

Regular monitoring of proteinuria (using urine protein/creatinine ratio), renal function, and complications of nephrotic syndrome is essential. Supportive care including dietary sodium restriction and management of oedema with diuretics may also be required.

First-line treatment for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in children is oral prednisolone for 4-8 weeks.
Calcineurin inhibitors are second-line therapy for steroid-resistant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
Regular monitoring of proteinuria is essential to assess treatment response in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
Q077-Oral-prednisolone.learning:
First-line treatment for focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in children is oral prednisolone for 4-8 weeks.
Calcineurin inhibitors are second-line therapy for steroid-resistant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
Regular monitoring of proteinuria is essential to assess treatment response in focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

Q061-Referral-for-genetic-testing-and-re.stem:
A seven-year-old boy presents to the General Practice clinic with a six-week history of facial swelling. This started with swelling around the eyes and was more noticeable in the mornings. Over the past two weeks, he has had an intermittent fever, and his mother has noticed that he has not been urinating as often as usual. She brought her child to the clinic five weeks ago, and the initial examination revealed bilateral pedal and facial oedema, along with a distended abdomen. At that time, the urine dipstick showed protein 3+ but no blood. The child was prescribed prednisolone at a standard dose for four weeks, but there has been no change in his condition, and if anything, his symptoms have become more severe.

On examination, he appears well with a pulse rate of 90/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and temperature 37.2°C. His face and legs are swollen. Abdominal examination reveals ascites.

Investigations reveal:

Serum albumin: 22 g/L (35-50)
Serum creatinine: 60 μmol/L (20-80)
Urine protein:creatinine ratio: 350 mg/mmol (<20)

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Evaluation for underlying infections or other systemic diseases
Supportive care with diuretics and dietary modifications
Referral for genetic testing and renal biopsy

Q061-Referral-for-genetic-testing-and-re.correctAnswer: Referral for genetic testing and renal biopsy
Q061-Referral-for-genetic-testing-and-re.rationale:
This child presents with classic features of nephrotic syndrome: oedema, proteinuria, and hypoalbuminaemia. The most appropriate next step in management is referral for genetic testing and renal biopsy. This is because the child has not responded to a four-week course of standard-dose prednisolone, which defines steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.

The urinalysis shows significant proteinuria (3+ on dipstick and urine protein:creatinine ratio of 350 mg/mmol) without haematuria. This pattern is typical for nephrotic syndrome and less consistent with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN), which typically presents with haematuria, red cell casts, and often hypertension.

In this scenario, genetic testing (typically via next-generation sequencing gene panels targeting podocyte genes such as NPHS1, NPHS2, and WT1) is highly useful alongside a biopsy. Identifying a pathogenic genetic variant confirms a monogenic cause for the steroid resistance. This is valuable because genetic forms of nephrotic syndrome generally do not respond to immunosuppressive therapies, allowing the clinician to cease these medications and avoid their significant toxicities. Furthermore, it helps predict prognosis, as genetic forms have a much lower risk of disease recurrence following a future kidney transplant compared to non-genetic forms, and can identify syndromic risks (such as nephroblastoma in WT1 variations).

Increasing the dose of prednisolone is not appropriate as the child has already failed to respond to a standard course, indicating steroid resistance. Continuing high-dose steroids without a clear diagnosis may lead to unnecessary side effects.

Evaluation for underlying infections or other systemic diseases is less likely to be helpful at this stage. While infections can trigger nephrotic syndrome, the persistent nature of symptoms despite steroid treatment suggests a primary renal pathology.

Supportive care with diuretics and dietary modifications may help manage symptoms but does not address the underlying cause. These measures are typically used in conjunction with specific treatment for nephrotic syndrome.

Plasmapheresis is not a first-line treatment for nephrotic syndrome and would not be considered without a specific diagnosis from a renal biopsy.

Genetic testing and renal biopsy are crucial in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome to identify the underlying cause, which could include conditions like focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, minimal change disease, or genetic forms of nephrotic syndrome. The results will guide appropriate treatment and provide prognostic information.

For childhood nephrotic syndrome, a renal biopsy is indicated for steroid resistance.
Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
Q061-Referral-for-genetic-testing-and-re.learning:
For childhood nephrotic syndrome, a renal biopsy is indicated for steroid resistance.
Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.

Q100-Serum-cortisol.stem:
A 45-year-old Aboriginal male from East Arnhem Land is referred to Renal Clinic with a two-week history of swollen legs and frothy urine. He has a medical history of hypertension and takes irbesartan and amlodipine. On examination, he appears unwell. His pulse rate is 78/min, blood pressure 149/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. He has pitting oedema to the level of the groin.

Investigations reveal:

Urinalysis: 3+ protein

Serum albumin: 20 g/L (35-50)

Total cholesterol: 7.2 mmol/L (2.0-5.5)

Serum creatinine: 130 μmol/L (60-110)

Renal biopsy light microscopy: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

Electron microscopy: Diffuse foot process effacement

The nephrologist recommends starting high-dose oral prednisolone.

Which one of the following tests is LEAST important to check before initiating steroid therapy?

options.text: Renal biopsy light microscopy: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
Electron microscopy: Diffuse foot process effacement

Q100-Serum-cortisol.rationale:
The population of the Top End of the Northern Territory has a high incidence of several infections. This is particularly pronounced in the immunosuppressed cohort e.g. patients on high-dose prednisolone >0.5mg/Kg/day for >14days, as well as patients undergoing chemotherapy or on other potent immunosuppressive agents.

Conditions such as disseminated strongyloidiasis, melioidosis, tuberculosis, scabies hyper-infestation and activation of hepatitis B virus infection can occur in immunosuppressed patients, and are generally more common in the Top End region compared to other parts of Australia. Hence, it is important to screen for such conditions prior to the commencement of high dose steroids.

Hepatitis B serology is crucial to check before starting immunosuppressive therapy, including steroids. Patients with chronic or occult hepatitis B infection are at risk of viral reactivation when immunosuppressed, which can lead to severe hepatitis and liver failure. This is particularly important in populations with a higher prevalence of hepatitis B.

Latent tuberculosis testing is essential to screen for latent tuberculosis infection. Steroid therapy can reactivate latent TB, leading to active disease. Identifying and treating latent TB before starting steroids is crucial to prevent this complication.

Strongyloides serology screening is important in this patient from an endemic area. Disseminated strongyloidiasis can be life-threatening. Screening and treating for Strongyloides before starting steroids is standard practice in patients from endemic regions.

HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) is important to check before starting steroid therapy. Steroids can cause or exacerbate hyperglycaemia, and knowing the baseline glycaemic status helps in monitoring and managing this side effect. This is particularly relevant in patients with risk factors for diabetes.

While serum cortisol can be useful in some situations to assess adrenal function, it is not routinely necessary before starting exogenous steroid therapy for most patients. The other tests mentioned are more critical for patient safety when initiating immunosuppression.

In summary, when starting high-dose steroid therapy, priority should be given to screening for infections that can be reactivated (hepatitis B, tuberculosis, strongyloidiasis) and assessing baseline metabolic status (diabetes). These tests are crucial for preventing potentially severe complications of immunosuppressive therapy.

The population of the Top End of the Northern Territory has a high incidence of several infections.
This is particularly pronounced in the immunosuppressed cohort e.g. patients on high-dose prednisolone >0.5mg/Kg/day for >14days, as well as patients undergoing chemotherapy or on other potent immunosuppressive agents.
Conditions such as disseminated strongyloidiasis, melioidosis, tuberculosis, scabies hyper-infestation and activation of hepatitis B virus infection can occur in immunosuppressed patients.

Q047-Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.stem:
A 55-year-old Indigenous female is referred to Renal Clinic with a two-week history of swollen legs and frothy urine. She has a medical history of hypertension and takes irbesartan and amlodipine. On examination, she appears unwell. Her pulse rate is 78/min, blood pressure 149/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. She has pitting oedema to the level of the groin.

Investigations reveal:

Urinalysis: 3+ protein

Serum albumin: 20 g/L (35-50)

Total cholesterol: 7.2 mmol/L (2.0-5.5)

Serum creatinine: 130 μmol/L (60-110)

Renal biopsy light microscopy: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

Electron microscopy: Diffuse foot process effacement

High-dose oral prednisolone is commenced.

Which one of the following medications should also be commenced?

options.text: Renal biopsy light microscopy: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
Electron microscopy: Diffuse foot process effacement

Q047-Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.rationale:
This patient has been diagnosed with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) based on renal biopsy findings. The nephrologist has recommended high-dose oral prednisolone (>20mg), which is a first-line treatment for FSGS presentations with nephrotic syndrome. When starting high-dose corticosteroids, it is important to consider prophylactic medications to prevent complications associated with steroid use, in particular their immunosuppressive properties at high doses.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) is crucial for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis in patients on high-dose immunosuppression. PJP can be a life-threatening complication in immunosuppressed patients.

Benzathine benzylpenicillin is incorrect. It is used to treat bacterial infections including group A Streptococcus which is associated with acute rheumatic fever, a condition with a higher prevalence in Indigenous Australians.

Insulin aspart (short-acting) and Insulin protaphane (intermediate-acting) are both incorrect. Steroids can certainly cause hyperglycaemia, although it would be inappropriate to start insulin immediately without a period of BSL monitoring first. Insulin protaphane is often used as the peak action typically matches the afternoon hyperglycaemia peak associated with steroid use.

Risedronate is incorrect. Whilst high-dose steroid use is a risk factor for osteoporosis, it would be inappropriate to prophylactically commence anti-resorptive therapy. Some clinicians may commence patients in high risk groups on prophylactic colecalciferol +/- calcium supplementation whilst on high-dose steroids.

High-dose oral prednisolone is a first-line treatment for primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) presenting with nephrotic syndrome.
Prophylactic medications are important when commencing high-dose corticosteroids to prevent complications.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is crucial in immunosuppressed patients.
Q047-Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.learning:
High-dose oral prednisolone is a first-line treatment for primary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) presenting with nephrotic syndrome.
